title: Wise Words
subtitle: WITH MARCO REYES  ·  STORY NIGHT

segments.head: TONIGHT: LYLE'S GARAGE
segments.author: Wise Words
lines: Good evening, everyone.
I'm Marco Reyes, and this is Wise Words.
Tonight's story is about Lyle Dempsey, a retired railroad conductor in Cheyenne, Wyoming.
For eleven years, not one car has fit in his two-car garage.
Then his wife Marlene said, Before the first snow, my car goes in that garage. Or you do.

segments.head: CHAPTER 1: THE AVALANCHE
segments.quote: Have nothing in your houses that you do not know to be useful, or believe to be beautiful.
segments.author: William Morris
lines: Lyle opened the door, and six lawn chairs fell on him.
Marlene taped a card to the wall, from William Morris, the English designer:
Have nothing in your houses that you do not know to be useful, or believe to be beautiful.
So every item got one question. Useful? Beautiful?
Three broken toasters. Neither.

segments.head: CHAPTER 2: THE WORKBENCH
segments.quote: The ability to simplify means to eliminate the unnecessary so that the necessary may speak.
segments.author: Hans Hofmann
lines: By day three, he wanted to quit. There was just so much stuff.
His daughter Sara texted him a line from Hans Hofmann, the painter:
The ability to simplify means to eliminate the unnecessary so that the necessary may speak.
So he kept going. And under forty years of junk, he found his dad's old oak workbench.

segments.head: CHAPTER 3: THE BOAT
segments.quote: Wealth is not his that has it, but his that enjoys it.
segments.author: Benjamin Franklin
lines: Then came the fishing boat. Lyle hadn't fished since the Clinton years.
Marlene read from his old Ben Franklin almanac:
Wealth is not his that has it, but his that enjoys it.
He didn't enjoy that boat. He just dusted it.
So he sold it to a young guy who went fishing the very next morning.

segments.head: CHAPTER 4: ACROSS THE STREET
segments.quote: Life's most persistent and urgent question is, 'What are you doing for others?'
segments.author: Martin Luther King Jr.
lines: Across the street, a young couple was expecting a baby.
Lyle remembered a line from Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.:
Life's most persistent and urgent question is, 'What are you doing for others?'
He carried over a crib, a high chair and two space heaters.
They cried. Lyle said it was the dust.

segments.head: CHAPTER 5: SALE DAY
segments.author: John Wooden
lines: Then came the garage sale. At six a.m., there was a line down the block.
Lyle started tossing out wrong prices. Then he remembered coach John Wooden:
Be quick, but don't hurry.
So he slowed down, smiled and counted the change twice.
By noon, the driveway was empty.

segments.head: CHAPTER 6: THE SWAP MEET
segments.quote: A man is rich in proportion to the number of things which he can afford to let alone.
segments.author: Henry David Thoreau
lines: The next Saturday, at the swap meet, Lyle saw a rusty anvil. Only twenty dollars.
His hand went to his wallet. Then he thought of Thoreau:
A man is rich in proportion to the number of things which he can afford to let alone.
He let the anvil alone.
That night, the first snow fell. Marlene's car was inside, and Lyle was at his dad's bench.

segments.head: THAT'S TONIGHT'S STORY
segments.quote: Keep what's useful. Clear the clutter. Enjoy it. Give. Slow down. Let it alone.
segments.author: Marco Reyes
lines: That's tonight's story.
Keep what's useful. Clear the clutter. Enjoy what you have. Give the rest. Slow down. And let some things alone.
My own closet still holds forty bow ties. All of them beautiful, of course.
I'm Marco Reyes. Good night.
